title: Passwords in the log pipeline
summary: A debugging change three weeks ago started shipping every request body to the log vendor.

brief.subject: I searched the logs for my own email and found my password
brief.body:
Hey,

I was in the log platform chasing a slow checkout and searched for my own email address to find my session. I found it. I also found my password, in plain text, in the event body.

I stopped searching at that point and came to you.

Someone added request bodies to the logger about three weeks ago, I think while debugging the checkout thing. It went in as a one-line change and nobody flagged it, me included — I reviewed it.

Worth knowing before you start: our retention is 400 days and search is open to everyone with a workspace seat. That is engineering, support, and the data science team.

Tomas
objectives: Find what is being written to the log pipeline and where it comes from
Work out the blast radius, including what already sits in the vendor’s storage
Decide what has to happen to the logs that have already been shipped

debrief.rootCause: A debugging change added `headers` and a serialised `req.body` to every logged event. The login route posts an email and a password in that body, and the key-rotation route posts the current API key, so both now arrive at the log platform in plain text. The `headers` field carries the `authorization` header and any session cookie alongside them. The validation on the login route is thorough, which is part of why the change read as harmless in review: the body is well-formed, and well-formed is not the same as safe to store.
debrief.businessImpact: Every password used to sign in during the last three weeks is now readable in a second system, by everyone with a seat on it, for 400 days — engineering, support, data science, and the vendor’s staff on request. Because people reuse passwords, the exposure is not limited to this product. Rotating our own secrets does nothing for a user whose password also opens their email. The API keys in the rotation route are in the same position, except those we can revoke ourselves.
debrief.remediation: Redact at the point of serialisation using an allowlist of fields that are safe to log, rather than a denylist of field names — a denylist fails the first time someone adds `passphrase` or `pin`. Then deal with what is already there: ask the vendor to purge the affected index rather than waiting out 400 days, revoke every API key seen in the rotation route, and tell the affected users to change their password, including anywhere they reused it. That last step is the one that is easy to argue out of and is the only one that helps the people actually at risk.

questions.prompt: Which lines put credentials into the log pipeline?

options.text: auth.routes.ts lines 13-16 — the login route parses the password out of the request body
logging.ts lines 11-16 — shipToLogService posts to an external endpoint over the network
requestLogger.ts lines 13 and 14 — the headers and the serialised request body are attached to every event
auth.routes.ts lines 27-29 — the rotate route reads currentKey without validating it

questions.explanation: Line 14 serialises whatever was posted, which on the login route is an email and a password. Line 13 attaches the headers, which carry the authorization header and the session cookie. The login route itself is doing nothing wrong — it has to receive a password to check one. The defect is that something downstream decided to keep a copy.
hints: The diff on this file is two lines long. Start there.
Ask what is actually inside `req.body` on the route that signs a user in.
One of the two lines exposes the credential the user typed; the other exposes the one their browser sends automatically.

questions.prompt: The log platform is a contracted vendor with a signed DPA. Why is this still a serious exposure?

options.text: The passwords now exist in a second system with 400-day retention and broad internal search access, and a password the user reuses elsewhere is beyond our power to contain
The events are sent over HTTPS to an endpoint outside our VPC, so they can be intercepted in transit
JSON.stringify does not escape control characters, so a crafted password can corrupt the log index
The vendor is in the EU, so storing credentials there is a transfer that the DPA does not cover

questions.explanation: A contract governs what the vendor may do with the data; it does not unstore it, shorten the retention, or narrow who inside our own company can search it. The part that reaches furthest is reuse: for any user whose password also opens their bank or their email, the harm we have created is somewhere we cannot reach, and no clause we sign changes that. The transit in option B is encrypted, and option D inverts the actual concern.
hints: A contract restricts what the vendor does. List the things it does not change.
Think about where else the same password is likely to work.

questions.prompt: What is the correct shape of the fix?

options.text: Drop any field named password, token or secret before the event is shipped
Log an allowlist of fields known to be safe, then purge what has already been shipped and get the affected users to change their password
Hash the request body before logging it, so the content is unreadable but still comparable
Stop logging bodies on the auth routes specifically, and leave the rest of the application logging as it is

questions.explanation: A denylist of field names is a guess about the future, and it loses the first time someone adds `passphrase`, `pin` or `answer` — an allowlist fails closed instead. The second half matters as much: the code fix stops the bleeding but does nothing about three weeks of credentials already sitting in a system with 400-day retention. Option D is the same denylist thinking applied to routes rather than fields, and the next route that takes a secret will not be on the list.
hints: One of these options guesses at the names of future secrets. The other decides what is safe to keep.
The code change stops new exposure. What deals with the exposure that has already happened?

ethicalChoices.text: Ship the redaction, then say plainly in writing that user passwords have been readable in a third-party system for three weeks, and push for a vendor purge and a message telling users to change any password they reused.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The redaction shipped the same day. The vendor purged the index within a week once someone asked them directly. The user message was rewritten four times because nobody wanted to say "your password was visible to our staff", and the version that went out said it anyway. Support took about 300 password resets and roughly forty angry replies. At the post-incident review the CTO’s note was that the three weeks were a process failure and the message was not.

ethicalChoices.text: Ship the redaction, and treat the three weeks already in the vendor’s storage as an accepted risk — the retention window will clear it eventually and nobody outside the company can search it.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The code was correct and the exposure stopped growing. Eight months later a contractor with a support seat left under difficult circumstances, and the question of what they could have searched had no good answer, because the credentials were still in the index and would be for another four months. The users were never told and never changed anything. The internal review found that the decision had been made by one engineer, in a ticket comment, on a Friday.

ethicalChoices.text: Ship the redaction and raise a ticket asking the vendor about purging, but leave the question of telling users to the security team rather than pressing it yourself.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The purge happened, a month later than it needed to, after the ticket was chased twice. The user notification was discussed and quietly dropped, on the reasoning that no evidence of misuse had been found — which was true, and was also a statement about what had been looked for. Nothing bad is known to have come of it. Your tech lead pointed out afterwards that "I raised it" and "I pushed for it" are different things, and that you had done the first.
